newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan army retreat from Kabul, Taleban advance.
newsitem.headline: Afghan army retreat from Kabul, Taleban advance.

text.p: Afghan government troops were leaving Kabul to avoid a "bloodbath" with Islamic rebels, and the country's besieged president was considering handing over power, deputy foreign minister Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai said.

Taleban Islamic militia appeared poised to capture the capital having seized the main government airbase north of Kabul and parts of the city, including its abandoned Khwaja Rawash airport, Taleban sources in neighbouring Pakistan said.
The minister said that the country's military commander, Ahmad Shah Masood, had gone north of the city, taking with him jet fighters and other military hardware.

The president, Burhanuddin Rabbani, was on the outskirts of the capital and would decide on Friday about a "transfer of power", he said in an interview with Reuters Television at the United Nations late on Thursday.
"Masood has decided to retreat to territory north of the city because he didn't want Kabul city to turn into a bloodbath," the minister said.

"The president is in the outskirts to the north and by tomorrow will announce his decision whether to leave the capital," he said adding that the president would take the advice of other members of his high council.
He said he thought "there will be a transfer of power, to whom we do not know," adding that he would be consulting with members of his high council.
He said he hoped that Afghanistan's former King, Zahir Shah, ousted in 1973 and now in Rome, would return to the country as even the Taleban would accept him in a leadership role.

A spokeswoman for U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros- Ghali, Sylvana Foa, told a news briefing at the United Nations that one U.N. and one International Committee of the Red Cross plane had airlifted 40 U.N. staff and aid workers out.
There were some 50 foreigners left in Kabul, three of them U.N. staff, she said.
Taleban sources said the militia had also taken Kabul's Soviet-built Microrayon housing complex in the east and the diplomatic Wazir Akbar Khan district in central Kabul.

The sources, quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), said troops loyal to President Rabbani were fleeing northwards, but his militia forces were resisting Taleban fighters near the presidential palace in central Kabul.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report, which also said the Taleban had taken Kohe Asmai hill, known as Television Hill, in the middle of Kabul.

While the airport in Kabul was made unusable by factional fighting, the Soviet-built Bagram, shared by jet fighters and civilian airliners, was the only base left giving the government an air link with the outside world.
Some civilians had fled the city on the road north earlier in the day in dozens of trucks and buses, but with a curfew in force most Kabul citizens stayed in their homes.

The Taleban, which emerged from obscurity two years ago and now controls most of Afghanistan, seeks to oust Rabbani and impose a strict Islamic order. Its leader Mullah Mohammad Omar said recently it had no ethnic or regional prejudices and only wanted to enforce Islamic sharia (law).
